Q: What's the difference between the TMP Input Field Line Types `MultiLineSubmit` and `MultiLineNewline`? A:

SingleLine is of course trivial: No multi lines, Enter means submit

MultiLineSubmit: Enter menas submit, Shift + Enter means new line instead

MultiLineNewLine Afaik means: Enter means new line! There is no built-in submit

In the latter you usually handle the submitting rather via a secondary additional UI button

Q: Can't synthesize when using generate block A:

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Let's test out that enthusiastic assertion, shall we?

I am really wanting to use a Generate block to do this so that it won't be as tedious and even expandable in the future.

This is an admirable and worthy goal.

The synthesis log message you showed is vague. However, when I try to compile your generate code with a simulator, I get error messages which clearly describe the problem with the code. The Verilog code has syntax errors. I see these errors on 2 different simulators.

This leads me to believe you have omitted the most important step in working with Verilog: running a simulation. That is where you need to begin to solve your problem.

This line is a problem:

assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];

That line is inside nested for loops. If you were to "unroll" the loops, you would end up with the same assign 36 times:

assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];
assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];
assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];
assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];
assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];
// ...
assign currentCol = squareTopLeftTemp[0];

Since you declared currentCol as a reg type, you are not allowed multiple procedural assignments to the same signal. Also, it is more common to use assign with the wire type. The errors go away if we use:

wire [9:0] currentCol; // starts at 144

However, you still have the 36 assignments, which is not what you wanted.

To make your debugging easier, start out with a smaller n, like n=2.

Q: Simple way to download Google Chrome/Chromium source code A:

Finally here I have the new and easy solution (Windows instructions)

  1. Install Git

  2. Install Visual Studio with these workloads and features:

    • Desktop development with C++

    • C++ ATL

    • C++ MFC

  3. Modify Windows SDK installation to include the "Debugging tools for Windows" feature

  4. Create directory C:\chromium_build

  5. Clone depot_tools and run update_depot_tools

C:\chromium_build> git clone https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/tools/depot_tools.git

C:\chromium_build> cd depot_tools

C:\chromium_build\depot_tools> update_depot_tools

  1. Close the command prompt, Set depot_tools to PATH, set DEPOT_TOOLS_WIN_TOOLCHAIN to 0, and open command prompt again

  2. Create a 'chromium' directory and then run these commands:

C:\chromium_build> md chromium

C:\chromium_build> cd chromium

C:\chromium_build\chromium> gclient config --name src https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git@138.0.7204.308

C:\chromium_build\chromium> echo|set /p="target_os = [ 'win' ]" >> .gclient

C:\chromium_build\chromium> gclient sync --nohooks --no-history
  1. Run hooks manually by running these commands:

C:\chromium_build\chromium> vpython3 -vpython-spec src/.vpython3 -vpython-tool install

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/landmines.py

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/third_party/depot_tools/update_depot_tools_toggle.py --disable

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/tools/remove_stale_files.py src/third_party/test_fonts/test_fonts.tar.gz src/third_party/node/node_modules.tar.gz src/third_party/tfhub_models

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/tools/remove_stale_pyc_files.py src/android_webview/tools src/build/android src/gpu/gles2_conform_support src/infra src/ppapi src/printing src/third_party/blink/renderer/build/scripts src/third_party/blink/tools src/third_party/catapult src/third_party/mako src/tools

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/vs_toolchain.py update --force

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/util/lastchange.py -o src/build/util/LASTCHANGE

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/util/lastchange.py -m GPU_LISTS_VERSION --revision-id-only --header src/gpu/config/gpu_lists_version.h

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/util/lastchange.py -m SKIA_COMMIT_HASH -s src/third_party/skia --header src/skia/ext/skia_commit_hash.h

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/build/util/lastchange.py -s src/third_party/dawn --revision src/gpu/webgpu/DAWN_VERSION

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/third_party/depot_tools/download_from_google_storage.py --no_resume --bucket chromium-browser-clang/rc -s src/build/toolchain/win/rc/win/rc.exe.sha1

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/tools/update_pgo_profiles.py --target=win32 update --gs-url-base=chromium-optimization-profiles/pgo_profiles

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/tools/update_pgo_profiles.py --target=win64 update --gs-url-base=chromium-optimization-profiles/pgo_profiles

C:\chromium_build\chromium> python3 src/v8/tools/builtins-pgo/download_profiles.py download --depot-tools src/third_party/depot_tools --check-v8-revision --quiet
  1. Create a args.gn file with these contents, and then save it to C:\chromium_build\chromium\src\out\Default\args.gn:

is_debug = false
is_component_build = false
is_official_build = true
clang_use_chrome_plugins=false
symbol_level = 0
blink_symbol_level = 0
enable_nacl=false
enable_iterator_debugging=false
enable_profiling=false
enable_resource_allowlist_generation = false
disable_fieldtrial_testing_config = true
  1. Run commands to build Chromium:

C:\chromium_build\chromium\src> gn gen out/Default

C:\chromium_build\chromium\src> ninja -C out/Default chrome -j 8

Q: Lexers vs. parsers A:

What parsers and lexers have in common:

  1. They read symbols of some alphabet from their input.

    • Hint: The alphabet doesn't necessarily have to be of letters. But it has to be of symbols which are atomic for the language understood by parser/lexer.

    • Symbols for the lexer: ASCII characters.

    • Symbols for the parser: the particular tokens, which are terminal symbols of their grammar.

  2. They analyse these symbols and try to match them with the grammar of the language they understood.

    • Here's where the real difference usually lies. See below for more.

    • Grammar understood by lexers: regular grammar (Chomsky's level 3).

    • Grammar understood by parsers: context-free grammar (Chomsky's level 2).

  3. They attach semantics (meaning) to the language pieces they find.

    • Lexers attach meaning by classifying lexemes (strings of symbols from the input) as the particular tokens. E.g., all these lexemes: *, ==, <=, ^ will be classified as "operator" token by the C/C++ lexer.

    • Parsers attach meaning by classifying strings of tokens from the input (sentences) as the particular nonterminals and building the parse tree. E.g., all these token strings: [number][operator][number], [id][operator][id], [id][operator][number][operator][number] will be classified as "expression" nonterminal by the C/C++ parser.

  4. They can attach some additional meaning (data) to the recognized elements.

    • When a lexer recognizes a character sequence constituting a proper number, it can convert it to its binary value and store with the "number" token.

    • Similarly, when a parser recognize an expression, it can compute its value and store with the "expression" node of the syntax tree.

  5. They all produce on their output a proper sentences of the language they recognize.

    • Lexers produce tokens, which are sentences of the regular language they recognize. Each token can have an inner syntax (though level 3, not level 2), but that doesn't matter for the output data and for the one which reads them.

    • Parsers produce syntax trees, which are representations of sentences of the context-free language they recognize. Usually it's only one big tree for the whole document/source file, because the whole document/source file is a proper sentence for them. But there aren't any reasons why parser couldn't produce a series of syntax trees on its output. E.g., it could be a parser which recognizes SGML tags stuck into plain-text. So it'll tokenize the SGML document into a series of tokens: [TXT][TAG][TAG][TXT][TAG][TXT]....

As you can see, parsers and tokenizers have much in common. One parser can be a tokenizer for other parser, which reads its input tokens as symbols from its own alphabet (tokens are simply symbols of some alphabet) in the same way as sentences from one language can be alphabetic symbols of some other, higher-level language. For example, if * and - are the symbols of the alphabet M (as Morse code symbols), then you can build a parser which recognizes strings of these dots and lines as letters encoded in the Morse code. The sentences in the language "Morse code" could be tokens for some other parser, for which these tokens are atomic symbols of its language (e.g., "English words" language). And these "English words" could be tokens (symbols of the alphabet) for some higher-level parser which understands "English sentences" language. And all these languages differ only in the complexity of the grammar. Nothing more.

So what's all about these "Chomsky's grammar levels"? Well, Noam Chomsky classified grammars into four levels depending on their complexity:

  • Level 3: Regular grammars

    They use regular expressions, that is, they can consist only of the symbols of alphabet (a,b), their concatenations (ab,aba,bbb, etc.), or alternatives (e.g., a|b).
    They can be implemented as finite-state automata (FSA), like Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) or better DFA (Deterministic Finite Automaton).

    Regular grammars can't handle with nested syntax, e.g. properly nested/matched parentheses (()()(()())), nested HTML/BBcode tags, nested blocks, etc. It's because state automata to deal with it should have to have infinitely many states to handle infinitely many nesting levels.

  • Level 2: Context-free grammars

    They can have nested, recursive, self-similar branches in their syntax trees, so they can handle with nested structures well.

    They can be implemented as state automaton with stack. This stack is used to represent the nesting level of the syntax. In practice, they're usually implemented as a top-down, recursive-descent parser which uses machine's procedure call stack to track the nesting level, and use recursively called procedures/functions for every non-terminal symbol in their syntax.

    But they can't handle with a context-sensitive syntax. E.g., when you have an expression x+3 and in one context this x could be a name of a variable, and in other context it could be a name of a function, etc.

  • Level 1: Context-sensitive grammars

  • Level 0: Unrestricted grammars
    Also called recursively enumerable grammars.

Q: RESTFUL API: Using path parameters vs query parameters A:

This answer is an attempt to provide some additional clarity.

Key Information = Web servers & clients conform to a specification.

The specification, lays out (among other things), a prescribed Request format and defined responses to different types of requests.
A URL is the visible form of the requests and has a specific structure under which requests can be made and data can be sent to the web server.
Web clients must conform to the standards/specifications so the web servers and clients can communicate.

  1. URL spec
    The URL, based on it's technical spec, is only made up of the following:
    - Scheme (HTTP, HTTPS, ...) the protocol
    - Authority (made of the following 3 items)

    • Userinfo (user:pass) ... not often used
    • Host (example.com or subdomain.example.com) the domain
    • Port (:1234)
      - Path (/homepage/about/, /index/, etc...) as defined, this references web pages
      - Query (?key=value&key2=value2&key3=value3 etc...) after the "?" there can be key value pairs
      - Fragment (#thisisafragment or #thisisanotherfragment) this is an anchor, which is an on page link)

  2. Libraries & Tools
    There are additional libraries/tools which can interface between the above and features the library has implemented.
    While these libraries can and often do, provide additional features or even change the intended use of a URL, they are only true when using the library/tool.
    - React (defines a concept of "path parameters" where the paths are overloaded to have the possibility of including parameters instead of representing just web pages)
    - Node.js Express (defines a concept of "route parameters" similar to react... but with a naming scheme that makes it more clear that the routing capabilities are adding the parameters, not the URL spec...)
    - etc...

  3. REST
    This is generally accepted (and referred to) as a scheme that utilizes existing parts of the capabilities in the technical specifications surrounding web communications upon which an API can be built.
    Specifically holding to the Request Methods defined as explained here: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods
    - GET = a standard request for information from the server
    - PUT = a request to add information sent to the server
    - DELETE = a request to delete information on the server
    - POST = a request to update information on the server
    There is more to this but it is not a formal technical spec for web servers and clients.
    More reading: https://twobithistory.org/2020/06/28/rest.html

  4. DEPENDS
    So, the end message is, where you put parameters and how you work with them, depends on the library/framework you are using them with/in.
    - If you are not using a framework or library that has some other concept for parameters then, the parameters you have available are the key value pairs listed after the "?" in a URL.
    - If you are using a framework or library that has some other concept of parameters in a URL then whatever the documentation says should be fine.
    (it's worth noting that path parameters and route parameters and similar are not referring to the technically specified location for parameter like data in the formal specs)

MORE RESOURCES

  • DOM URL methods, etc...: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URL

  • DOM Location methods (also URL related): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Location

  • HTTP Headers: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers

  • HTTP Request methods (same link as above): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods

Q: add message to python logging no matter which log level A: 
import logging
ALWAYS_LEVEL = 100  # Higher than CRITICAL (50)
logging.addLevelName(ALWAYS_LEVEL, "ALWAYS")

def log_always(message):
    logging.log(ALWAYS_LEVEL, message)

log_always("This message ignores all standard thresholds.")
